Power Flow Analysis

Complete guide to AC power flow in Powerful.jl.

Basic Usage

using Powerful, PowerFlowData

case = PowerFlowData.parse_network("cases/ieee14.raw")
sys = SystemModel(case)
prob = ACPowerFlowProblem(sys)
sol = solve(prob, NewtonRaphson())

See Getting Started for explanation of each step.

Formulations

Power flow equations can be written in different mathematical forms. Powerful.jl supports two AC formulations.

PowerInjection (Default)

Uses polar coordinates with power balance equations.

Variables:

  • θ: Voltage angle at each bus
  • V: Voltage magnitude at each bus

Equations:

Pᵢ = Vᵢ ∑ⱼ Vⱼ(Gᵢⱼcos(θᵢ-θⱼ) + Bᵢⱼsin(θᵢ-θⱼ)) = 0
Qᵢ = Vᵢ ∑ⱼ Vⱼ(Gᵢⱼsin(θᵢ-θⱼ) - Bᵢⱼcos(θᵢ-θⱼ)) = 0

Where:

  • Pᵢ, Qᵢ: Net active/reactive power at bus i
  • Gᵢⱼ, Bᵢⱼ: Conductance/susceptance of admittance matrix Y
  • θᵢ, Vᵢ: Voltage angle/magnitude at bus i

Usage:

prob = ACPowerFlowProblem(sys)  # Default
# or explicit:
prob = ACPowerFlowProblem(sys, PowerInjection())

When to use: Default choice for well-conditioned systems.

CurrentInjection

Uses rectangular coordinates with current balance equations.

Variables:

  • Vᵣ: Real part of bus voltage
  • Vᵢ: Imaginary part of bus voltage

Equations:

Iᵣ = ∑ⱼ (Gᵢⱼ·Vᵣⱼ - Bᵢⱼ·Vᵢⱼ) = 0
Iᵢ = ∑ⱼ (Gᵢⱼ·Vᵢⱼ + Bᵢⱼ·Vᵣⱼ) = 0

Where:

  • Iᵣ, Iᵢ: Net real/imaginary current at bus i
  • Vᵣ, Vᵢ: Real/imaginary voltage components

Why rectangular coordinates?

The polar form (PowerInjection) involves division by voltage magnitude:

P = V·(...) / V  ← Numerical issues when V ≈ 0

The rectangular form (CurrentInjection) avoids this:

Iᵣ = G·Vᵣ - B·Vᵢ  ← Linear in voltage components

This gives better numerical conditioning near voltage collapse.

Usage:

prob = ACPowerFlowProblem(sys, CurrentInjection())
sol = solve(prob, NewtonRaphson())

When to use: Poorly conditioned systems, heavy loading, voltage collapse scenarios.

Comparison

AspectPowerInjectionCurrentInjection
CoordinatesPolar (θ, V)Rectangular (Vᵣ, Vᵢ)
JacobianMixed θ/V derivativesUniform Vᵣ/Vᵢ derivatives
ConditioningStandardBetter near low voltage
SpeedSlightly fasterComparable
Use caseNormal operationStressed conditions

Key point: Both give identical physical results. The difference is numerical behavior during convergence.

Formulation Example

# Try PowerInjection first
prob_pi = ACPowerFlowProblem(sys, PowerInjection())
sol_pi = solve(prob_pi, NewtonRaphson())

if !sol_pi.converged
    @warn "PowerInjection failed to converge"

    # Fall back to CurrentInjection
    prob_ci = ACPowerFlowProblem(sys, CurrentInjection())
    sol_ci = solve(prob_ci, NewtonRaphson())

    if sol_ci.converged
        println("CurrentInjection succeeded!")
    end
end

Algorithms

Choose the solution algorithm based on your needs.

NewtonRaphson (Default)

Full Newton-Raphson with sparse Jacobian.

sol = solve(prob, NewtonRaphson())

How it works:

  1. Evaluate residuals: g(y)
  2. Build Jacobian: J = ∂g/∂y (sparse matrix)
  3. Solve linear system: J·Δy = -g using KLU
  4. Update: y ← y + Δy
  5. Check convergence: ||g|| < tol

When to use: Default choice. Fast and reliable for most systems.

Options:

# Use different linear solver
sol = solve(prob, NewtonRaphson(linear_solver=CUDSSSolver()))  # GPU

# Tighter tolerance
sol = solve(prob, NewtonRaphson(abstol=1e-10))

# More iterations
sol = solve(prob, NewtonRaphson(maxiters=50))

RobustNewton

Uses NonlinearSolve.jl backend with automatic globalization.

sol = solve(prob, RobustNewton())

How it differs:

  • Automatic trust region / line search
  • More sophisticated convergence strategies
  • Better for difficult cases

When to use: When NewtonRaphson fails to converge.

Trade-off: Slightly slower (~20-30%) but more robust.

FastDecoupledXB

Fast decoupled power flow using XB variant.

sol = solve(prob, FastDecoupledXB())

How it works:

Decouples P-θ and Q-V equations:

ΔP ≈ B' · Δθ  (active power - angle)
ΔQ ≈ B'' · ΔV (reactive power - voltage)

Where B', B'' are constant susceptance matrices.

Approximations:

  1. cos(θᵢ - θⱼ) ≈ 1 (small angle differences)
  2. sin(θᵢ - θⱼ) ≈ θᵢ - θⱼ
  3. Qᵢ ≈ -Bᵢᵢ·Vᵢ (local approximation)
  4. r << x (resistance negligible)

Advantages:

  • Very fast (2-3× faster than Newton-Raphson)
  • Constant matrices (factor once, reuse)
  • Good for transmission networks

Limitations:

  • Less accurate for distribution networks (high r/x)
  • May need more iterations
  • Not suitable for heavy loading

When to use: Large transmission systems where speed matters and r/x is small.

Algorithm Comparison

using BenchmarkTools

# Same problem, different algorithms
@btime solve($prob, NewtonRaphson())     # ~2.5 ms, 4 iterations
@btime solve($prob, RobustNewton())      # ~3.2 ms, 5 iterations
@btime solve($prob, FastDecoupledXB())   # ~1.2 ms, 6 iterations

Advanced Options

AMD Reordering

Reorder variables for better sparse factorization.

prob = ACPowerFlowProblem(sys, PowerInjection();
                          addressing=AMDAddressing())
sol = solve(prob, NewtonRaphson())

Why: Reduces fill-in during LU factorization → faster solves.

When to use: Large systems (>1000 buses) where Jacobian factorization dominates.

GPU Acceleration

Use CUDA for large-scale systems.

using CUDA, CUDSS

prob = ACPowerFlowProblem(sys, PowerInjection(); array_type=CuArray)
sol = solve(prob, NewtonRaphson(linear_solver=CUDSSSolver()))

Requirements:

  • NVIDIA GPU with CUDA support
  • CUDSS.jl package

When to use: Very large systems (>10,000 buses) where GPU overhead pays off.

Warm Starting

Use previous solution as initial guess for faster convergence.

# Solve base case
prob = ACPowerFlowProblem(sys)
sol = solve(prob, NewtonRaphson())

# Modify system (use load at pure PQ bus to see voltage change)
sys.models.PQ.pl[3] *= 1.2  # Load 3 at Bus 4
sys.models.PQ.ql[3] *= 1.2

# Create new problem with warm start
prob_new = ACPowerFlowProblem(sys; initial_guess=sol.dae.y)
sol_new = solve(prob_new, NewtonRaphson())

# Converges faster (fewer iterations)

When to use: Parameter sweeps, contingency analysis, time-series.

Note: To observe voltage changes, modify loads at pure PQ buses (no generators). PV buses maintain constant voltage.

Convergence Diagnostics

Check Convergence

if sol.converged
    println("Success: $(sol.iterations) iterations")
    println("Final residual: $(sol.residual_norm)")
else
    @warn "Failed to converge"
    println("Iterations: $(sol.iterations)")
    println("Final residual: $(sol.residual_norm)")
end

Common Convergence Issues

Problem: Divergence (residual increasing)

Causes:

  • Infeasible operating point (too much load, not enough generation)
  • Voltage collapse (system near stability limit)
  • Bad initial guess

Solutions:

  1. Check power balance: ∑Pgen ≈ ∑Pload + losses
  2. Try CurrentInjection formulation
  3. Try RobustNewton algorithm
  4. Reduce loading incrementally

Problem: Slow convergence (many iterations)

Causes:

  • Poorly conditioned Jacobian
  • Nearly flat solution surface
  • Ill-conditioned system data

Solutions:

  1. Check for very small impedances (branches)
  2. Check for unrealistic setpoints
  3. Try FastDecoupledXB for speed

Multi-Island Systems

Systems with disconnected components are automatically detected and solved.

Automatic Approach (Recommended)

# Auto-detect and solve islands (default behavior)
prob = ACPowerFlowProblem(sys)  # Automatically detects islands
sol = solve(prob, NewtonRaphson())

# Returns MultiIslandSolution if multiple islands detected
# Access variables transparently - automatic island lookup
v1 = get_var(sol, :Bus, :v, (1,))  # Finds bus 1 in whichever island contains it
v8 = get_var(sol, :Bus, :v, (8,))  # Finds bus 8 automatically

How it works:

  1. ACPowerFlowProblem calls split_islands(sys) internally
  2. If multiple islands found, creates ACPowerFlowProblem{F, Vector{SystemModel}}
  3. solve() solves each island independently
  4. Returns MultiIslandSolution with transparent variable access

Manual Approach

For explicit control, use split_islands() directly:

# Manually check and split
result = split_islands(sys)

if result isa SystemModel
    # Single island - solve normally
    prob = ACPowerFlowProblem(result)
    sol = solve(prob, NewtonRaphson())
else
    # Multiple islands - solve each separately
    islands = result  # Vector{SystemModel}

    solutions = [solve(ACPowerFlowProblem(island), NewtonRaphson())
                 for island in islands]

    # Access from specific island solutions
    v1 = get_var(solutions[1], :Bus, :v, (1,))
    v8 = get_var(solutions[2], :Bus, :v, (8,))
end

Disabling Auto-Split

# Preserve old behavior (only solve first island)
prob = ACPowerFlowProblem(sys; auto_split=false)
sol = solve(prob, NewtonRaphson())

Key points:

  • Auto-split is enabled by default (auto_split=true)
  • Each island must have its own slack bus (bus type 3)
  • MultiIslandSolution provides transparent access across all islands
  • Variable access automatically searches islands to find the requested key

Accessing Results

Quick Access

# Access single variable
v = get_var(sol, :Bus, :v, (1,))     # Voltage at bus 1
θ = get_var(sol, :Bus, :theta, (1,)) # Angle at bus 1

# Get all values for a variable
all_v = get_all_vars(sol, :Bus, :v)  # All bus voltages

# Get as dictionary
v_dict = get_vars_dict(sol, :Bus, :v)  # Dict{key => value}

Generate Reports

# Collect results as table
bus_data = collect_model_table(sol, :Bus)

# Convert to DataFrame
using DataFrames
df = DataFrame(bus_data)

See Accessing Results for complete API reference, including:

  • External key formats
  • Multi-island transparent access
  • Advanced indexing
  • Report customization

Examples

Parameter Sweep

# Sweep load levels
load_factors = 0.8:0.1:1.2
results = []
prev_sol = nothing

for factor in load_factors
    # Scale all loads
    sys.models.PQ.pl .*= factor
    sys.models.PQ.ql .*= factor

    # Create problem with warm start
    if isnothing(prev_sol)
        prob = ACPowerFlowProblem(sys)
    else
        prob = ACPowerFlowProblem(sys; initial_guess=prev_sol.dae.y)
    end

    sol = solve(prob, NewtonRaphson())

    if sol.converged
        # Record min voltage
        v_min = minimum(get_all_vars(sol, :Bus, :v))
        push!(results, (factor=factor, v_min=v_min))
        prev_sol = sol  # Save for next iteration
    else
        @warn "Diverged at factor=$factor"
        break
    end

    # Reset for next iteration
    sys.models.PQ.pl ./= factor
    sys.models.PQ.ql ./= factor
end

Contingency Analysis

# Base case
prob_base = ACPowerFlowProblem(sys)
sol_base = solve(prob_base, NewtonRaphson())

# Try opening each branch
for i in 1:length(sys.models.Branch)
    # Open branch i
    original_status = sys.models.Branch.st[i]
    sys.models.Branch.st[i] = 0

    # Create new problem with warm start from base case
    prob = ACPowerFlowProblem(sys; initial_guess=sol_base.dae.y)
    sol = solve(prob, NewtonRaphson())

    if !sol.converged
        @warn "Contingency $i: Branch outage causes divergence"
    else
        # Check voltage violations
        v_dict = get_vars_dict(sol, :Bus, :v)
        violations = filter(p -> p[2] < 0.95 || p[2] > 1.05, v_dict)

        if !isempty(violations)
            @warn "Contingency $i: Voltage violations at buses $(keys(violations))"
        end
    end

    # Restore branch
    sys.models.Branch.st[i] = original_status
end
